title: After a death
translation: Nothing is as sad as what comes after a death.

For the forty-nine days of mourning, the family moves out to some mountain village, crowded into a small, awkward place, all doing the rites together, and it's hectic. The days go by faster than anything. On the last day everyone is very cold. Nobody says much. Each of them packs up their things, looking very efficient, and they all go their separate ways. Back home, there's surely even more to be sad about.
And people say things like "Careful, don't do this or that, it's bad luck for the family." At a time like this? It makes you think less of people.

Years go by, and it's not that anyone forgets. But as the saying goes, "the dead grow more distant every day". It probably doesn't hurt the way it did at the time. People chat about nothing and even laugh.

The body is buried somewhere lonely in the mountains, and people visit only on the proper days. Soon the grave marker is covered in moss and buried in fallen leaves, and the only visitors are the evening wind and the moon at night.

That's while someone is still alive to remember them. Those people die too, and the next generations only know the dead from stories. Do they feel anything? Then even the memorial rites stop, and nobody knows whose grave it is, not even the name. Someone with real feeling might be moved by the grass that comes back every spring. In the end, even the pine by the grave that moaned in the wind is cut up for firewood before it reaches a thousand years, and the old grave is ploughed into a rice field, until not even its shape is left.

literal: There is nothing as sad as the aftermath of a person's death.
During the period of mourning, moving to a mountain village or the like, many people staying together in an inconvenient, cramped place and performing the rites for the dead together: it is hectic.
The way the days pass quickly is like nothing else.
On the final day, very coldly, without speaking to each other, each one cleverly packing up their things, they scatter and part.
After returning to their original homes, surely there will be even more that is sad.
That they say things like 'Such-and-such, oh dear, is a thing to avoid for the sake of the survivors': amid all this, why such things? The human heart still seems unpleasant.

Even after years and months pass, it is not that one forgets at all, but as it is said, 'Those who have gone grow more distant day by day', and though that is so, perhaps one does not feel as at that time, for they talk of trivial things and even laugh.

The remains are laid in the eerie mountains, and when one visits only on the proper days, soon the grave post is mossy and buried by falling leaves, and only the evening storm and the night moon are there to call.
That is while there are people who remember and miss them.
But they too soon die, and do the later generations, who only hear of it, feel it as moving?

And when even the rites for the dead have stopped, not even knowing whose it is by name, only the spring grass of each year a person of feeling might see as moving, but in the end even the pine that sobbed in the storm, before waiting a thousand years, is broken up for firewood, and the old grave is ploughed and becomes a field.
That even its shape is gone is sad.

notes.text: {中陰|ちゆういん}: the forty-nine days after death, during which, in Buddhist belief, the dead pass between this life and the next. The family held rites every seven days.

notes.quote: 我かしこげに物ひきしたため
notes.text: かしこげ: 'looking clever, looking competent'. Each person busy with their own packing. The coldness is in the efficiency.

notes.quote: 跡のため忌むなる事ぞ
notes.text: Superstitions about what would bring bad luck to the survivors. In the middle of grief, people worry about bad luck. うたて: 'unpleasant'.

A line from a Chinese poem in the Wen Xuan (see section 13): 'those who have gone grow more distant every day'. It became a Japanese proverb, still used today in the form {去|さ}る{者|もの}は{日々|ひび}に{疎|うと}し.
{卒都婆|そとば}: a wooden post or board on a grave, cut in the shape of a stupa and written with sutra words. They still stand in Japanese graveyards today.

notes.quote: ふるき墳はすかれて田となりぬ
notes.text: Also from the same Chinese poem (one of the 'Nineteen Old Poems' in the Wen Xuan): 'old graves are ploughed into fields, pines and cypresses are cut for firewood'. Kenkō follows its images closely.

notes.quote: その形だになくなりぬるぞ悲しき
notes.text: ぞ … き closes the section: 'that not even its shape remains is sad'. The translation ends on the image, the shape disappearing, and lets the sadness stay in it.
